claim: Cycling cells maintain centriole number at precisely two per cell in part by limiting their duplication to S phase under the control of the cell cycle machinery.
source: Cycling cells maintain centriole number at precisely two per cell in part by limiting their duplication to S phase under the control of the cell cycle machinery.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cell cycle control of centriole duplication.

claim: Postmitotic multiciliated cells (MCCs) uncouple centriole assembly from cell cycle progression and produce hundreds of centrioles in the absence of DNA replication.
source: In contrast, postmitotic multiciliated cells (MCCs) uncouple centriole assembly from cell cycle progression and produce hundreds of centrioles in the absence of DNA replication to serve as basal bodies for motile cilia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCC biology that is widely accepted in the field.

claim: Cdk2 is required in MCCs to initiate motile ciliogenesis.
source: We use transgenic mice and primary airway epithelial cell culture to show that Cdk2, the kinase responsible for the G1 to S phase transition, is also required in MCCs to initiate motile ciliogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic mice and cell culture experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cdk2 is coupled with cyclins E and A2 during cell division.
source: While Cdk2 is coupled with cyclins E and A2 during cell division, cyclin A1 is required during ciliogenesis, contributing to an alternative regulatory landscape that facilitates centriole amplification without DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cdk2-cyclin interactions during the cell cycle.

claim: Cyclin A1 is required during ciliogenesis.
source: While Cdk2 is coupled with cyclins E and A2 during cell division, cyclin A1 is required during ciliogenesis, contributing to an alternative regulatory landscape that facilitates centriole amplification without DNA replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ccna1 expression patterns and knockout mouse phenotypes.

claim: Cyclin A1 contributes to an alternative regulatory landscape that facilitates centriole amplification without DNA replication.
source: While Cdk2 is coupled with cyclins E and A2 during cell division, cyclin A1 is required during ciliogenesis, contributing to an alternative regulatory landscape that facilitates centriole amplification without DNA replication.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and represents a speculative model.

claim: A pair of centrioles and surrounding pericentriolar material comprise the centrosome.
source: A pair of centrioles, and surrounding pericentriolar material, comprise the centrosome (Vertii et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In interphase, one of the centrioles can serve as basal body for a primary cilium.
source: In interphase, one of the centrioles can serve as basal body for a primary cilium while the pericentriolar material is a principal site for cytoplasmic microtubule nucleation and organization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about centriole function.

claim: Pericentriolar material is a principal site for cytoplasmic microtubule nucleation and organization.
source: In interphase, one of the centrioles can serve as basal body for a primary cilium while the pericentriolar material is a principal site for cytoplasmic microtubule nucleation and organization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about centrosome function.

claim: In mitosis, centrosomes regulate the assembly and orientation of the mitotic spindle.
source: In mitosis, centrosomes regulate the assembly and orientation of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about centrosome function during mitosis.

claim: Dysfunction of centrioles or associated structures results in developmental and adult tissue maintenance defects.
source: Dysfunction of centrioles or associated structures results in developmental and adult tissue maintenance defects (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2011), which have been linked to human disease, notably ciliopathies and cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Centriole dysfunction has been linked to human disease, notably ciliopathies and cancer.
source: Dysfunction of centrioles or associated structures results in developmental and adult tissue maintenance defects (Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2011), which have been linked to human disease, notably ciliopathies and cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In dividing cells, centriole generation occurs in S phase of the cell cycle when exactly two new (daughter) centrioles assemble, each next to an existing (mother) centriole.
source: In dividing cells, centriole generation occurs in S phase of the cell cycle when exactly two new (daughter) centrioles assemble, each next to an existing (mother) centriole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Fırat-Karalar and Stearns, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Extra centrioles can lead to abnormal mitoses.
source: Control of centriole number is important for proper cellular function: extra centrioles can lead to abnormal mitoses (Yang et al., 2008) or give rise to extra primary cilia that results in defective signaling (Mahjoub and Stearns, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Extra centrioles can give rise to extra primary cilia that results in defective signaling.
source: Control of centriole number is important for proper cellular function: extra centrioles can lead to abnormal mitoses (Yang et al., 2008) or give rise to extra primary cilia that results in defective signaling (Mahjoub and Stearns, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Multiciliated cells (MCCs) of the airway, ependymal, middle ear and oviduct epithelia assemble dozens to hundreds of centrioles in a single postmitotic cytoplasm to act as basal bodies to motile cilia.
source: Multiciliated cells (MCCs) of the airway, ependymal, middle ear and oviduct epithelia break the rules that govern centriole formation in dividing cells, as they assemble, depending on cell type, dozens to hundreds of centrioles in a single postmitotic cytoplasm to act as basal bodies to motile cilia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Meunier and Azimzadeh, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: MCC fate is acquired in a Notch signaling-dependent manner, with cells experiencing Notch activation becoming secretory cells and cells not experiencing Notch activation progressing down the MCC pathway.
source: MCC fate is acquired in a Notch signaling-dependent manner, with cells experiencing Notch activation becoming secretory cells and cells not experiencing Notch activation progressing down the MCC pathway (Tsao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both MCCs and dividing cells produce apparently structurally identical centrioles.
source: Yet, both MCCs and dividing cells produce apparently structurally identical centrioles, and the MCC pathway appears to rely on many known cell cycle regulated centrosome duplication factors such as the Plk4 kinase and structural components including Sass6 and Centrin proteins (Vladar and Stearns, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research supported by a citation.

claim: The MCC pathway appears to rely on many known cell cycle regulated centrosome duplication factors such as the Plk4 kinase and structural components including Sass6 and Centrin proteins.
source: Yet, both MCCs and dividing cells produce apparently structurally identical centrioles, and the MCC pathway appears to rely on many known cell cycle regulated centrosome duplication factors such as the Plk4 kinase and structural components including Sass6 and Centrin proteins (Vladar and Stearns, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Timely entry and progression through S phase is regulated by Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (Cdk2) complexed with cyclins E or A2.
source: Timely entry and progression through S phase is regulated by Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (Cdk2) complexed with cyclins E or A2 (Hochegger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation supported by a citation.

claim: The G1 to S phase transition occurs when mitogenic stimulation leads to activation of the Cdk4/6-cyclin D complex.
source: The G1 to S phase transition occurs when mitogenic stimulation leads to activation of the Cdk4/6-cyclin D complex, which acts to dissociate the E2F1 transcription factor from the Dp1 and Retinoblastoma (Rb) proteins, leading to E2F1 activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Cdk4/6-cyclin D complex acts to dissociate the E2F1 transcription factor from the Dp1 and Retinoblastoma (Rb) proteins, leading to E2F1 activation.
source: The G1 to S phase transition occurs when mitogenic stimulation leads to activation of the Cdk4/6-cyclin D complex, which acts to dissociate the E2F1 transcription factor from the Dp1 and Retinoblastoma (Rb) proteins, leading to E2F1 activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: E2F1 turns on key S phase genes, notably cyclins E and A2 and DNA synthesis factors.
source: E2F1 turns on key S phase genes, notably cyclins E and A2 and DNA synthesis factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Cyclin E binding leads to activation of Cdk2.
source: Cyclin E binding leads to activation of Cdk2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Cdk2, coupled to cyclin A2, initiates entry into and controls progression through S phase and the twin events of centriole and DNA duplication.
source: Then Cdk2, coupled to cyclin A2 (which further phosphorylates E2F1) initiates entry into and controls progression through S phase and the twin events of centriole and DNA duplication (Hinchcliffe et al., 1999; Lacey et al., 1999; Matsumoto et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many cell cycle regulators localize to the centrosome.
source: The precise events that link the cell cycle machinery to centriole duplication are not yet clear, however, many regulators localize to the centrosome (Kodani et al., 2015) and may control Plk4 stability and activity (Korzeniewski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cell cycle regulators may control Plk4 stability and activity.
source: The precise events that link the cell cycle machinery to centriole duplication are not yet clear, however, many regulators localize to the centrosome (Kodani et al., 2015) and may control Plk4 stability and activity (Korzeniewski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on prior research supported by a citation.

claim: The initiation of the MCC gene expression program depends on a transcriptional complex (EMD complex) comprising the E2F4 or E2F5 transcription factor, a Geminin family transcriptional activator (Mcidas or Gmnc) and Dp1.
source: The initiation of the MCC gene expression program depends on a transcriptional complex (EMD complex) comprising the E2F4 or E2F5 transcription factor, a Geminin family transcriptional activator (Mcidas or Gmnc) and Dp1 (Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The EMD complex is highly similar in make up to the E2F1/Rb/Dp1 complex that controls G1 to S phase progression.
source: This complex is highly similar in make up to the E2F1/Rb/Dp1 complex that controls G1 to S phase progression, which suggests the existence of universal cell cycle regulatory mechanisms to create a permissive environment for centriole assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity of the complexes.

claim: The similarity between EMD and E2F1/Rb/Dp1 complexes suggests the existence of universal cell cycle regulatory mechanisms to create a permissive environment for centriole assembly.
source: This complex is highly similar in make up to the E2F1/Rb/Dp1 complex that controls G1 to S phase progression, which suggests the existence of universal cell cycle regulatory mechanisms to create a permissive environment for centriole assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural similarity.

claim: The Myb and p73 transcription factors turn on further MCC genes downstream of EMD.
source: Downstream of EMD, the Myb and p73 transcription factors, also well known for their cell cycle functions (Allocati et al., 2012), turn on further MCC genes (Tan et al., 2013; Marshall et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The G2 to M phase cell cycle machinery, including Cdk1, regulates intermediate stages of ciliogenesis in ependymal MCCs.
source: Finally, the G2 to M phase cell cycle machinery, including Cdk1 was shown regulate intermediate stages of ciliogenesis in ependymal MCCs (Al Jord et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cdk2 is required for initiating and sustaining the MCC gene expression program during ciliogenesis.
source: Here, we show that downstream of MCC fate acquisition, Cdk2 is required to initiate and maintain the MCC gene expression program during ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: MCCs driven to differentiate in the absence of Cdk2 activity fail to undergo ciliogenesis.
source: Consistently, MCCs driven to differentiate in the absence of Cdk2 activity fail to undergo ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Cdk2 appears to function during ciliogenesis together with Cyclin A1 (Ccna1).
source: Unlike in dividing cells, Cdk2 appears to function during ciliogenesis together with Cyclin A1 (Ccna1), a cognate cyclin thought to activate Cdk2 in meiotic cell cycles (Joshi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data and prior knowledge about Ccna1.

claim: Cyclin A1 is a cognate cyclin thought to activate Cdk2 in meiotic cell cycles.
source: Unlike in dividing cells, Cdk2 appears to function during ciliogenesis together with Cyclin A1 (Ccna1), a cognate cyclin thought to activate Cdk2 in meiotic cell cycles (Joshi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cdk2 activity is a universal regulator of centriole assembly.
source: In sum, our results indicate that Cdk2 activity is universal regulator of centriole assembly, and the involvement of Ccna1, a noncanonical binding partner in somatic cells, and likely other factors enable it to function in a postmitotic cell and drive centriole amplification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The involvement of Ccna1 and likely other factors enable Cdk2 to function in a postmitotic cell and drive centriole amplification.
source: In sum, our results indicate that Cdk2 activity is universal regulator of centriole assembly, and the involvement of Ccna1, a noncanonical binding partner in somatic cells, and likely other factors enable it to function in a postmitotic cell and drive centriole amplification.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: MTECs treated with Purvalanol A, Roscovitine, NU6140 and Cdk2 Inhibitor III from ALI + 0 to ALI + 4 d blocked ciliogenesis.
source: While untreated cultures contained many MCCs, we found that all four Cdkis blocked ciliogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Cdki treated MTECs failed to form centrioles, deuterosomes or ciliary axonemes.
source: To characterize this phenotype, we labeled cells with antibodies against structural and regulatory components of the ciliogenesis pathway, and found that Cdki treated MTECs failed to form centrioles (ac. α-Tub, Odf2, Pericentrin, Sass6, and Plk4), deuterosomes (Ccdc67, also known as Deup1) or ciliary axonemes (ac. α-Tub), indicating an early ciliogenesis arrest (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cdki treated cells did not express the MCC TFs Foxj1 and Myb.
source: We found that Cdki treated cells did not express the MCC TFs Foxj1 and Myb (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cdki treated cells had no detectable levels of MCC TFs and ciliary genes were not upregulated.
source: Using qRT-PCR, untreated cells showed strong upregulation of both MCC TFs and ciliary genes at ALI + 4 d compared to confluent, but not yet differentiating cells (ALI-1d or day 4 of culture), whereas Cdki treated cells had no detectable levels of MCC TFs and ciliary genes were not upregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Cdki treatment blocks motile ciliogenesis at an early step of the pathway at the level of MCC gene expression.
source: Cdki treatment therefore blocks motile ciliogenesis at an early step of the pathway at the level of MCC gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Ciliogenesis arrest was fully reversible for all Cdkis, as MTECs released from ALI + 0 to +4 d Cdki treatment were robustly ciliated by ALI + 8 d.
source: Ciliogenesis arrest was fully reversible for all Cdkis, as MTECs released from ALI + 0 to +4 d Cdki treatment were robustly ciliated by ALI + 8 d (Figure 1B,D for NU6140 and Purvalanol A, others not shown).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Cdki treatment had no effect on overall epithelial morphology as judged by E-cadherin antibody labeling of apical cell-cell junctions or on the presence of primary cilia.
source: Cdki treatment had no effect on overall epithelial morphology as judged by E-cadherin antibody labeling of apical cell-cell junctions or on the presence of primary cilia (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The Cdk1/2-specific Purvalanol A and Roscovitine and the Cdk2-specific NU6140 and Cdk2 Inhibitor III compounds robustly inhibited ciliogenesis.
source: We found the while the Cdk1/2-specific Purvalanol A and Roscovitine and the Cdk2-specific NU6140 and Cdk2 Inhibitor III compounds robustly inhibited ciliogenesis, the Cdk1 inhibitor RO3306 had no effect (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: The Cdk1 inhibitor RO3306 had no effect on ciliogenesis.
source: We found the while the Cdk1/2-specific Purvalanol A and Roscovitine and the Cdk2-specific NU6140 and Cdk2 Inhibitor III compounds robustly inhibited ciliogenesis, the Cdk1 inhibitor RO3306 had no effect (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Lentiviral expression of a dominant negative HA-Cdk2 (D145N) construct blocked ciliogenesis.
source: Moreover, lentiviral expression of a dominant negative HA-Cdk2 (D145N) construct also blocked ciliogenesis, while the expression of wildtype HA-Cdk2 or GFP had no effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Expression of wildtype HA-Cdk2 or GFP had no effect on ciliogenesis.
source: Moreover, lentiviral expression of a dominant negative HA-Cdk2 (D145N) construct also blocked ciliogenesis, while the expression of wildtype HA-Cdk2 or GFP had no effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Cdk2 is required for initiation of the motile ciliogenesis pathway.
source: Thus, we conclude that Cdk2 is required for initiation of the motile ciliogenesis pathway, consistent with its previously described role in centriole assembly in S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: MTECs treated with DAPT alone had a two-fold increase in MCCs compared to untreated cells.
source: MTECs treated with DAPT alone had a two-fold increase in MCCs compared to untreated cells as more cells evaded Notch activation and remained in the MCC pathway (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: DAPT treatment was not able to induce MCCs in the presence of NU6140.
source: However, DAPT treatment was not able to induce MCCs in the presence of NU6140 (Figure 2A), indicating that even cells directed toward the MCC fate by Notch inhibition still require Cdk2 activation to continue this progression.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Cells directed toward the MCC fate by Notch inhibition still require Cdk2 activation to continue this progression.
source: However, DAPT treatment was not able to induce MCCs in the presence of NU6140 (Figure 2A), indicating that even cells directed toward the MCC fate by Notch inhibition still require Cdk2 activation to continue this progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: NU6140 treated MTECs lacked Foxj1+ MCCs but contained as many TRRAP+ cells as untreated MTECs at the same stage.
source: We found that while Nu6140 treated MTECs lacked Foxj1+ MCCs, they contained as many TRRAP+ cells as untreated MTECs at the same stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: TRRAP does not act downstream of Cdk2 activation in prospective MCCs.
source: This indicates that in prospective MCCs, TRRAP does not act downstream of Cdk2 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cdk2 acts either downstream of or in parallel to TRRAP in the initiation of the MCC gene expression program.
source: Cdk2 therefore acts either downstream of or in parallel to TRRAP in the initiation of the MCC gene expression program (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The appearance of TRRAP expression in the absence of Cdk2 activity indicates the adoption of the MCC cell fate.
source: Furthermore, the appearance of TRRAP expression in the absence of Cdk2 activity indicates the adoption of the MCC cell fate, thus separating Cdk2 activity from the MCC cell fate decision.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: MTECs infected with lentivirus containing Mcidas and treated with NU6140 from ALI + 0 to 4d were able to carry out the complete motile ciliogenesis pathway.
source: MTECs infected at d3 of culture with lentivirus containing the MCC TF Mcidas, then treated with NU6140 from ALI + 0 to 4d were able to carry out the complete motile ciliogenesis pathway as judged by Foxj1 expression and the presence of cilia (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Cultures expressing Myb or Foxj1 under NU6140 treatment did not undergo ciliogenesis.
source: Cultures expressing Myb or Foxj1 under these conditions did not undergo ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: NU6140 treated cells expressing Foxj1 had nuclear or nucleo-cytoplasmic Foxj1 signal, but never made cilia.
source: NU6140 treated cells expressing Foxj1 had nuclear or nucleo-cytoplasmic Foxj1 signal, but never made cilia (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Cdk2 acts upstream of Mcidas.
source: This suggests that Cdk2 acts upstream of Mcidas and raises the possibility that Mcidas or one of its binding partners may be a target of Cdk2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mcidas or one of its binding partners may be a target of Cdk2.
source: This suggests that Cdk2 acts upstream of Mcidas and raises the possibility that Mcidas or one of its binding partners may be a target of Cdk2.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: The expression of Mcidas and Myb, but not Foxj1, was sufficient to drive motile ciliogenesis in untreated MTECs.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the expression of Mcidas and Myb (Stubbs et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2013), but not Foxj1 (You et al., 2004), was sufficient to drive motile ciliogenesis in untreated MTECs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data and consistent with prior reports.

claim: The Cdk2 requirement is downstream of the Notch-dependent cell fate decision and upstream of EMD in the MCC gene expression pathway for initiating ciliogenesis.
source: Our results place the Cdk2 requirement downstream of the Notch-dependent cell fate decision and upstream of EMD in the MCC gene expression pathway for initiating ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Acute Cdki treatment from ALI + 3 to ALI + 4 d resulted in an immediate ciliogenesis arrest.
source: To test if it is also required for the sustained expression of ciliary genes, we treated MTECs after the onset of ciliogenesis, from ALI + 3 to ALI + 4 d, with NU6140 (acute treatment). Acute Cdki treatment resulted in an immediate ciliogenesis arrest (Figure 3A–B), indicating that Cdk2 is not only required to initiate, but also to sustain the pathway.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Cdk2 is not only required to initiate, but also to sustain the ciliogenesis pathway.
source: To test if it is also required for the sustained expression of ciliary genes, we treated MTECs after the onset of ciliogenesis, from ALI + 3 to ALI + 4 d, with NU6140 (acute treatment). Acute Cdki treatment resulted in an immediate ciliogenesis arrest (Figure 3A–B), indicating that Cdk2 is not only required to initiate, but also to sustain the pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cdki treatment blocked the transition from a heterogeneous population of ciliating cells to a population with fewer ciliating and more mature MCCs.
source: Untreated cultures consistently transition from a heterogeneous population of ciliating cells with some mature MCCs to a population with fewer ciliating and more mature MCCs between ALI + 3 to 4d (Figure 3A–B). We found that Cdki treatment blocked this transition and cells arrested at all stages of ciliogenesis (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Cells arrested at all stages of ciliogenesis under Cdki treatment.
source: We found that Cdki treatment blocked this transition and cells arrested at all stages of ciliogenesis (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Acute Cdki treatment did not result in a statistically significant decrease in the Myb+/Foxj1- population and the Myb-/Foxj1+ population failed to increase.
source: However, we did not detect a statistically significant decrease in the Myb+/Foxj1- population and the Myb-/Foxj1+ population failed to increase under Cdki treatment (Figure 3C), indicating that cells failed to progress in the ciliogenesis pathway.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: The expression of structural and regulatory ciliary genes (Ccdc67, Plk4, Sass6 and Cetn2) declined upon Cdki treatment.
source: We also found that the expression of structural and regulatory ciliary genes (Ccdc67, Plk4, Sass6 and Cetn2) declined upon Cdki treatment, which suggests that continued Cdk2 activity is required to maintain MCC gene expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Continued Cdk2 activity is required to maintain MCC gene expression.
source: We also found that the expression of structural and regulatory ciliary genes (Ccdc67, Plk4, Sass6 and Cetn2) declined upon Cdki treatment, which suggests that continued Cdk2 activity is required to maintain MCC gene expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: NU6140 treatment had no effect on mature MCCs.
source: We again rule out that the NU6140 arrest is simply nonspecific injury to MCCs as treatment had no effect on mature MCCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Total Cdk2 levels did not change during ciliogenesis at the protein or transcript level.
source: Although total Cdk2 levels did not change during ciliogenesis at the protein or transcript level, we detected a peak in Cdk2 bearing the activating Thr160 phosphorylation (Gu et al., 1992) by Western blot at ALI+2 to +4d, a time interval that is enriched for MCCs in early ciliogenesis (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data.

claim: A peak in Cdk2 bearing the activating Thr160 phosphorylation was detected by Western blot at ALI+2 to +4d.
source: Although total Cdk2 levels did not change during ciliogenesis at the protein or transcript level, we detected a peak in Cdk2 bearing the activating Thr160 phosphorylation (Gu et al., 1992) by Western blot at ALI+2 to +4d, a time interval that is enriched for MCCs in early ciliogenesis (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data.

claim: The presence of nuclear Cdk2 in ciliating MCCs and the enrichment of phospho-Thr160 Cdk2 in ciliating MTECs indicates that Cdk2 is active during early ciliogenesis.
source: The presence of nuclear Cdk2 in ciliating MCCs and the enrichment of phospho-Thr160 Cdk2 in ciliating MTECs indicates that Cdk2 is active during early ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: HA-Cdk2 localized to centrioles in both ciliating and mature MCCs.
source: Interestingly, we found that HA-Cdk2 also localized to centrioles in both ciliating and mature MCCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cdk2 can localize to the centrosome in cycling cells.
source: However, others have reported that Cdk2 can localize to the centrosome in cycling cells (Kodani et al., 2015), and that it has centrosomal phosphotargets (Chen et al., 2002; Okuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cdk2 has centrosomal phosphotargets.
source: However, others have reported that Cdk2 can localize to the centrosome in cycling cells (Kodani et al., 2015), and that it has centrosomal phosphotargets (Chen et al., 2002; Okuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both the nuclear and centriolar pools of Cdk2 may be involved in ciliogenesis regulation.
source: Thus, both the nuclear and centriolar pools of Cdk2 may be involved in ciliogenesis regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the localization data.

claim: Ccna1 showed a large increase, followed by a decline in expression during motile ciliogenesis.
source: We examined the expression of Ccna1, Ccna2, Ccne1 and Ccne2 during motile ciliogenesis (Figure 5A) and detected a large increase, followed by a decline in expression for Ccna1 and a more modest increase in expression for Ccne1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Ccne1 showed a more modest increase in expression during motile ciliogenesis.
source: We examined the expression of Ccna1, Ccna2, Ccne1 and Ccne2 during motile ciliogenesis (Figure 5A) and detected a large increase, followed by a decline in expression for Ccna1 and a more modest increase in expression for Ccne1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: The timing of peak Ccna1 and Ccne1 expression correlates with the indicators of Cdk2 activation during ciliogenesis.
source: The timing of their peak expression correlates with the indicators of Cdk2 activation during ciliogenesis (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the timing of different experimental observations.

claim: Ccne2 did not show statistically significant change in expression during ciliogenesis.
source: Ccne2 did not show statistically significant change and consistent with a postmitotic state, only a negligible amount of Ccna2 was detected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Only a negligible amount of Ccna2 was detected during ciliogenesis, consistent with a postmitotic state.
source: Ccne2 did not show statistically significant change and consistent with a postmitotic state, only a negligible amount of Ccna2 was detected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data and interpreted in the context of cell cycle state.

claim: Only Ccna1 matched the expression profile of strong upregulation followed by a decline during ciliogenesis.
source: The majority of ciliary genes show strong upregulation followed by a decline in expression during ciliogenesis (ex. Cetn2), and this pattern can be used to identify transcripts important for the process (Hoh et al., 2012). Although we cannot rule out a role for the other canonical cyclins, only Ccna1 matched this profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge about ciliary gene expression patterns.

claim: An enrichment of the Ccna1 protein was found during ciliogenesis.
source: In addition to Ccna1 transcripts, we also found an enrichment of the Ccna1 protein during ciliogenesis (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data.

claim: Ccna1 expression was restricted to MCCs.
source: To test if Ccna1 expression is restricted to MCCs, we carried out qRT-PCR in sorted MCCs and non-MCCs obtained by FACS from the Foxj1-EGFP mouse line (Ostrowski et al., 2003) and found that Ccna1 expression was restricted to MCCs (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data from sorted cells.

claim: The negligible amount of Ccna2 expression derives from non-MCCs.
source: This analysis also revealed that the negligible amount of Ccna2 expression derives from non-MCCs and that Ccne1 was detected in both populations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data from sorted cells.

claim: Ccne1 was detected in both MCC and non-MCC populations.
source: This analysis also revealed that the negligible amount of Ccna2 expression derives from non-MCCs and that Ccne1 was detected in both populations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data from sorted cells.

claim: The MCC-specific pool of Ccne1 showed the characteristic rise and fall of expression during ciliogenesis.
source: The MCC-specific pool of Ccne1 also showed the characteristic rise and fall of expression during ciliogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Ccne1 may also regulate ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding that leads to a speculative hypothesis.

claim: A genomic fragment within the human CCNA1 promoter can drive Luciferase reporter gene expression in response to the MCC TFs E2F4 (but only in the presence of MCIDAS), FOXJ1 and MYB.
source: Consistent with its MCC-specific expression, we demonstrated that a genomic fragment within the human CCNA1 promoter can drive Luciferase reporter gene expression in response to the MCC TFs E2F4 (but only in the presence of MCIDAS), FOXJ1 and MYB (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) in 293T/17 cells, similar to a FOXJ1 promoter fragment previously shown to display MCC-restricted expression (Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by luciferase assay data.

claim: Transfection of MCC TFs into 293T/17 cells turned on the expression of endogenous human CCNA1, FOXJ1 and CETN2.
source: Furthermore, transfection of the same MCC TFs into 293T/17 cells turned on the expression of endogenous human CCNA1, and also FOXJ1 and CETN2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Ccna1 is a target of the MCC gene expression program during ciliogenesis.
source: Ccna1 is therefore a target of the MCC gene expression program during ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Employing Ccna1 to drive a noncanonical somatic event may drive centriole assembly in MCCs, but not other Cdk2-driven events such as DNA replication.
source: We hypothesize that employing this A-type cyclin to drive a noncanonical somatic event may drive centriole assembly in MCCs, but not other Cdk2-driven events such as DNA replication.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Ccna1-GFP was strongly nuclear in ciliating MCCs.
source: We found that similar to Cdk2, Ccna1-GFP was present in the nucleus during ciliogenesis. It was strongly nuclear in ciliating MCCs (Figure 6A) while mature MCCs had much lower overall levels of Ccna1-GFP in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Mature MCCs had much lower overall levels of Ccna1-GFP in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: We found that similar to Cdk2, Ccna1-GFP was present in the nucleus during ciliogenesis. It was strongly nuclear in ciliating MCCs (Figure 6A) while mature MCCs had much lower overall levels of Ccna1-GFP in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Endogenous Ccna1 showed nuclear localization in ciliating MCCs.
source: Using a Ccna1 antibody that specifically recognized Ccna1-GFP by Western blot and immunolabeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), we confirmed the nuclear localization of endogenous Ccna1 in ciliating MCCs.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Endogenous Ccna1 signal was not detected in mature MCCs.
source: Unlike with Ccna1-GFP, we did not detect endogenous signal in mature MCCs (Figure 6B), which may be due to antibody issues.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with a caveat about potential technical limitations.

claim: Ccna1 may undergo proteasomal degradation at the end of ciliogenesis.
source: Alternatively, it may indicate the proteasomal degradation of Ccna1 at the end of ciliogenesis, which may be overcome to some extent by continuous lentiviral expression.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Endogenous Ccna1 gene expression is suppressed by both chronic (ALI + 0 to+4 d) and acute (ALI + 3 to+4 d) Cdki treatment.
source: We found that similar to other ciliary genes, endogenous Ccna1 gene expression is suppressed by both chronic (ALI + 0 to+4 d) and acute (ALI + 3 to+4 d) Cdki treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Upon lentiviral co-expression, Cdk2-HA and Ccna1-GFP colocalized in the nucleus.
source: Upon lentiviral co-expression, Cdk2-HA and Ccna1-GFP colocalized in the nucleus and Ccna1 was also detected at the centrioles (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ccna1 was detected at the centrioles upon lentiviral co-expression with Cdk2.
source: Upon lentiviral co-expression, Cdk2-HA and Ccna1-GFP colocalized in the nucleus and Ccna1 was also detected at the centrioles (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ccna1-GFP localization depends on Cdk2 activity.
source: Moreover, we found that Ccna1-GFP localization depends on Cdk2 activity (Figure 6A), as Ccna1-GFP failed to accumulate in the nucleus in MTECs under chronic Cdki treatment that blocks the initiation of motile ciliogenesis, nor was it able to exit the nucleus under acute Cdk inhibition that arrests MCCs at intermediate stages of ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ccna1-GFP failed to accumulate in the nucleus in MTECs under chronic Cdki treatment.
source: Moreover, we found that Ccna1-GFP localization depends on Cdk2 activity (Figure 6A), as Ccna1-GFP failed to accumulate in the nucleus in MTECs under chronic Cdki treatment that blocks the initiation of motile ciliogenesis, nor was it able to exit the nucleus under acute Cdk inhibition that arrests MCCs at intermediate stages of ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ccna1-GFP was not able to exit the nucleus under acute Cdk inhibition.
source: Moreover, we found that Ccna1-GFP localization depends on Cdk2 activity (Figure 6A), as Ccna1-GFP failed to accumulate in the nucleus in MTECs under chronic Cdki treatment that blocks the initiation of motile ciliogenesis, nor was it able to exit the nucleus under acute Cdk inhibition that arrests MCCs at intermediate stages of ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cdk2 and Ccna1 function as a complex to regulate motile ciliogenesis in MCCs.
source: These results support a model in which, as in cycling cells, Cdk2 and Ccna1 function as a complex to regulate motile ciliogenesis in MCCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Ccna1 knockout mice are viable, but male-sterile due to the requirement for Ccna1 in the meiotic divisions of the male germline.
source: Ccna1 knockout mice are viable, but male-sterile due to the requirement for Ccna1 in the meiotic divisions of the male germline (Liu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ccna1-/- epithelia contained an increased number of dome-shaped, possibly secretory cells.
source: Ccna1-/- epithelia also contained an increased number of dome-shaped, possibly secretory cells, which may indicate further dysfunction in these airways (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with a speculative interpretation.

claim: No difference in the fraction of MCCs was found in Ccne1; Ccne2 double knockout mice.
source: In comparison, we examined Ccne1; Ccne2 double knockout mice (Geng et al., 2003) and found no difference in the fraction of MCCs. (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data.

claim: Ccna1 is required for motile ciliogenesis.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that Ccna1 is required for motile ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings from knockout mice.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ccna1 and Cdk2 either separately or together is not sufficient to drive the motile ciliogenesis pathway.
source: Although the ectopic expression of Ccna1 and Cdk2 either separately or together is not sufficient to drive the motile ciliogenesis pathway (Figure 1E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and not shown), our results are consistent with Cdk2 acting together with Ccna1 and possibly other cyclins upon MCC fate acquisition to activate the MCC gene expression program.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Cdk2 acts together with Ccna1 and possibly other cyclins upon MCC fate acquisition to activate the MCC gene expression program.
source: Although the ectopic expression of Ccna1 and Cdk2 either separately or together is not sufficient to drive the motile ciliogenesis pathway (Figure 1E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and not shown), our results are consistent with Cdk2 acting together with Ccna1 and possibly other cyclins upon MCC fate acquisition to activate the MCC gene expression program.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cdk2 activity is required to create a permissive environment for centriole generation in both dividing cells and MCCs.
source: In sum, our results show that Cdk2 activity is required to create a permissive environment for centriole generation in either context.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Ccna1 regulates meiosis in mammals and plants.
source: Of note, Ccna1 regulates meiosis in mammals and plants (Liu et al., 1998; d'Erfurth et al., 2010), another event in which centrioles are generated in the absence of DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Meiosis is an event in which centrioles are generated in the absence of DNA replication.
source: Of note, Ccna1 regulates meiosis in mammals and plants (Liu et al., 1998; d'Erfurth et al., 2010), another event in which centrioles are generated in the absence of DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Ccna1 may be degraded at or near the conclusion of motile ciliogenesis, possibly as a regulatory step in the pathway.
source: By analogy to cell cycle progression, we speculate that Ccna1 may be degraded at or near the conclusion of motile ciliogenesis, possibly as a regulatory step in the pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to cell cycle regulation.

claim: The different phenotypes between Ccna1 mice and Cdki treatment could represent different responses to a chronic loss of Ccna1 in vivo compared to the acute inhibition of Cdk activity in vitro.
source: Ccna1 mice showed a reduction in MCC number but not the complete block to ciliogenesis observed with Cdki treatment. The different phenotypes could represent different responses to a chronic loss of Ccna1 in vivo compared to the acute inhibition of Cdk activity in vitro.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The different phenotypes between Ccna1 mice and Cdki treatment may be due to partial redundancy with other cyclins.
source: We also speculate that it may be due to partial redundancy with other cyclins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Ccno is an important regulator of ciliogenesis downstream of the EMD complex.
source: Recent studies identified Ccno as an important regulator of ciliogenesis downstream of the EMD complex (Wallmeier et al., 2014), and although it is not known whether Ccno can activate Cdk2, it could conceivably also act partially redundantly with Ccna1.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ccno could conceivably act partially redundantly with Ccna1.
source: Recent studies identified Ccno as an important regulator of ciliogenesis downstream of the EMD complex (Wallmeier et al., 2014), and although it is not known whether Ccno can activate Cdk2, it could conceivably also act partially redundantly with Ccna1.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Ccp110 dissociates from the mother centriole distal end upon phosphorylation by Cdk2 to allow primary cilium growth.
source: Centrosomal Cdk2 targets include Ccp110, which dissociates from the mother centriole distal end upon phosphorylation to allow primary cilium growth (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ccp110 is present and required for motile ciliogenesis.
source: Ccp110 is present and required for motile ciliogenesis (Song et al., 2014), and the centriolar pool of Cdk2 may be regulating motile axoneme elongation in MCCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The centriolar pool of Cdk2 may be regulating motile axoneme elongation in MCCs.
source: Ccp110 is present and required for motile ciliogenesis (Song et al., 2014), and the centriolar pool of Cdk2 may be regulating motile axoneme elongation in MCCs.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on prior knowledge and the findings.

claim: Nucleophosmin 1 (Npm1), a Cdk2 substrate that shows both nuclear and centriolar localization, has been suggested as a link between Cdk2 activity and centrosome duplication.
source: Nucleophosmin 1 (Npm1), a Cdk2 substrate that shows both nuclear and centriolar localization, has been suggested as a link between Cdk2 activity and centrosome duplication (Okuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Forced expression of Mcidas in the presence of inhibited Cdk2 can sustain ciliogenesis.
source: We note that forced expression of Mcidas in the presence of inhibited Cdk2 can sustain ciliogenesis, suggesting that putative Cdk2 activity at replicating centrioles may not be absolutely required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Putative Cdk2 activity at replicating centrioles may not be absolutely required for ciliogenesis.
source: We note that forced expression of Mcidas in the presence of inhibited Cdk2 can sustain ciliogenesis, suggesting that putative Cdk2 activity at replicating centrioles may not be absolutely required.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The near normal viability of the Cdk2 knockout mouse revealed that other Cdks and Cdk-independent events are capable of driving cell cycle progression.
source: The near normal viability of the Cdk2 knockout mouse (Berthet et al., 2003) revealed that other Cdks and Cdk-independent events are capable of driving cell cycle progression, at least in the context of chronic Cdk2 absence.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The Cdk1-APC/C mitotic oscillator promotes intermediate phases of centriole replication in MCCs without stimulating mitosis.
source: The Cdk1-APC/C mitotic oscillator was recently shown to promote intermediate phases of centriole replication in MCCs without stimulating mitosis (Al Jord et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cdk2 plays a role in initiating the MCC gene expression program, the precursor to centriole assembly.
source: We demonstrate that Cdk2 plays a role in initiating the MCC gene expression program, the precursor to centriole assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Cdk2 acts downstream of the Notch signaling event and either downstream of, or in parallel with, TRRAP, and upstream of the EMD complex.
source: We support our placement of Cdk2 at this point in the regulatory hierarchy by demonstrating that it acts downstream of the Notch signaling event and either downstream of, or in parallel with, TRRAP, an early regulator of ciliogenesis, and upstream of the EMD complex that initiates and sustains MCC gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cdk1 and Cdk2 redundancy at centrioles may explain why a ciliogenesis phenotype was not detected with the Cdk1-specific RO3306 inhibitor.
source: Cdk1 and Cdk2 redundancy at centrioles may explain why we did not detect a ciliogenesis phenotype with the Cdk1-specific RO3306 inhibitor as observed by Al Jord et al.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The study by Al Jord et al. was chiefly carried out in ependymal MCCs, which make many fewer MCCs, and may reflect an alternative Cdk requirement.
source: As that study was chiefly carried out in ependymal MCCs, which make many fewer MCCs, it may also reflect an alternative Cdk requirement.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Cdk2 activity is required to create a permissive environment for centriole generation in both dividing cells and MCCs.
source: In sum, our results show that Cdk2 activity is required to create a permissive environment for centriole generation in either context.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Emerging studies point to the involvement of universal centriole assembly factors and events, including common regulators and biogenesis steps, and MCC-specific features.
source: Emerging studies point to the involvement of universal centriole assembly factors and events, including common regulators and biogenesis steps, and MCC-specific features, like the use of deuterosomes and transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is a summary of current knowledge in the field.
